summary: Deep technical workshop to align on benchmark methodology for runtime performance across hosted/dedicated/private (VPC/on-prem). Action items: share harness, run baseline on customer infra, schedule pilot kickoff.
topics:
- Benchmark goals and success criteria
- Prompt set design and representativeness (seq lengths, instruction vs chat)
- Load generation: concurrency, QPS, RPS, open vs closed loop
- Warmup and KV cache priming strategies
- Batching behavior and tail latency tradeoffs
- Quantization impacts on latency/throughput/quality
- VPC/on-prem network variability and perf isolation
- Metrics to collect (p50/p90/p99 latency, throughput, GPU utilization, token cost)

transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we're gonna run through a benchmark methodology workshop today, focus on runtime, VPC, KV cache, batching, quantization, the usual. Michael that's you, right?
[00:08] Michael: Yeah hi, thanks Samir, appreciate it. We want to make sure whatever we run is apples-to-apples, we care about p99 latency but also cost, and we run on our VPC.
[00:17] Leah: Cool, maybe quick agenda — prompt sets, load generation, warmup, KV cache priming, quant profiles, metrics and runbook.
[00:25] Laura: Sounds good. One thing up front, our infra is air-gapped-ish, so on-prem network variability matters.
[00:31] Priya: Also we have 3 production prompt classes: short single-turn user prompts (~16 tokens), medium instruction prompts (~64 tokens), and long chat context (~512 tokens). We can share examples.
[00:42] Samir: Perfect. When we say apples-to-apples I mean same model weights, same tokenizer, same seqlen limits and same warmup patterns, right?
[00:49] Michael: Exactly. We just want to avoid comparing a quantized variant to a full fp16 unless we're explicit.
[00:56] Leah: Right and we usually run these axes: model variant (fp16 vs int8/4bit), batching window (10ms, 25ms, 50ms), concurrency levels (1, 8, 32), and KV cache hit rates (cold, warm, hot).
[01:06] Laura: Quick q: how do you recommend priming the KV cache for a realistic hit rate? We saw big diffs in prior tests.
[01:12] Samir: Good question. We define a warmup phase where we replay a representative set of traffic at slightly higher QPS for N minutes until the KV hit ratio stabilizes. We instrument kv-hit-rate and per-token latency. Typically 5–15 minutes depending on model and sequence lengths.
[01:25] Priya: And what about prefix caching vs full KV? Our app uses long-lived sessions so prefix reuse is common.
[01:30] Leah: We track prefix reuse separately. For long-chat sessions prefix reuse dramatically reduces per-token compute because KV cache avoids recomputing prior layers. In benchmarks we include scenarios: no cache, session-level cache, and global prefix cache.
[01:44] Michael: Network variability: VPC cross-subnet latency can add jitter, how do we control for that?
[01:49] Samir: We recommend colocating load generator in same VPC subnet or using the same NAT path, run multiple trials and report median and p99 with confidence intervals. Also capture system metrics: NIC drops, retransmits.
[02:01] Laura: For on-prem, we have bursts of noisy neighbor traffic on the fabric — will that skew results?
[02:06] Leah: It can. That's why we advise running a baseline under minimal cluster load and then an isolation test with synthetic noise to quantify sensitivity.
[02:13] Michael: Prompt set design — we want to reuse our real requests but also have synthetic stress prompts?
[02:18] Samir: Yes, use a stratified sampling: production samples for representativeness plus a small set of synthetic edge cases (max seqlen, worst-case attention patterns). Also vary target output lengths to capture generation cost.
[02:30] Priya: How do you measure apples-to-apples across quantization? We saw quality regressions at 4-bit on some prompts.
[02:36] Leah: We pair throughput/latency metrics with quality evals — a small eval set scored for correctness or log-prob differences. For QC we run automated evals and a human spot-check on a sample. Keep quant config documented.
[02:47] Michael: On batching: what batch sizes are realistic for low latency SLOs?
[02:51] Leah: It depends on the batching window and target p99. For sub-200ms p99, small windows (10–20ms) and small effective batch sizes are typical. If you're optimizing throughput/cost, larger windows with higher batch sizes improve utilization but raise tail latency. We'll propose a few bucketed configs to test.
[03:07] Laura: Any guidance on continuous batching vs synchronous batching?
[03:11] Samir: Our runtime supports continuous batching to assemble requests quickly while respecting latency windows. For benching, run both modes and capture latency distribution; continuous batching often gives better average throughput without catastrophic tails, but needs careful window tuning.
[03:23] Michael: For load generation, open-loop vs closed-loop — which do you recommend?
[03:26] Leah: Both. Open-loop (fixed RPS) stresses the system and surfaces queueing behavior; closed-loop (fixed concurrency) reflects client-perceived latency under backpressure. For apples-to-apples, run matched open-loop scenarios across both envs at same target RPS, and closed-loop at same concurrency.
[03:40] Priya: Warm-up length again — is 5 minutes enough for large models?
[03:43] Samir: For small test models maybe, but for long-chat with KV priming and caching, we usually do 10–15 minutes and confirm KV hit-rate plateau. Document warmup policy in the runbook.
[03:53] Michael: What telemetry should we collect beyond p50/p90/p99 and throughput?
[03:57] Leah: GPU utilization, GPU memory footprint, GPU compute stalls, RPC latencies, batch sizes seen, kv-hit ratio, tokenization time, and system level metrics (CPU, disk, NIC). Also capture model-level logs — kernel launches and allocator stats if possible.
[04:13] Laura: On security: for VPC tests we'll need KMS integration for keys. Any special consideration for the benchmark harness?
[04:19] Samir: You can run with a test KMS key or local HSM mock. We'll ensure the harness supports fetching credentials from your KMS. For on-prem, we support HSM/KMS integrations but keys shouldn't be exported.
[04:31] Michael: Cost modeling — can you provide a worksheet mapping throughput to GPU-hours and token costs?
[04:34] Leah: Yes we'll produce a cost/latency projection spreadsheet that maps measured throughput to estimated GPU-hours and per-token cost given instance types and quantization profiles. We'll include an amortized cost for KV cache effects.
[04:46] Priya: About sequence length distribution — our prod is heavy tail, do you recommend bucketing by seqlen?
[04:51] Samir: Definitely. Create at least three buckets: short (<32), medium (32–256), long (>256). Report metrics per bucket and overall weighted by production frequency. That reveals when long sequences dominate GPU-memory or latency.
[05:03] Michael: When comparing hosted vs VPC vs on-prem, how do you ensure same model and kernel selection?
[05:08] Leah: Use the same model artifact (checksum) and disable automatic kernel switching if that would introduce variability, or at least document kernel versions. Make sure quantization pipeline uses identical steps (same calibration data, same compilation flags).
[05:20] Laura: Any pitfalls to avoid when measuring p99? We sometimes see single outliers from OS scheduling.
[05:24] Samir: Yes, isolate noisy system processes, pin CPUs if possible, and run multiple trials. Use trimmed statistics and report median with interquartile ranges and a p99 over multiple runs.
[05:36] Priya: For KV cache experiments, do you recommend synthetic keys or replay from production keys?
[05:41] Leah: Replay from production is best for representativeness, but ensure PII is sanitized. Synthetic keys can be useful for controlled hit-rate studies.
[05:51] Michael: Let's talk about the harness — does Redwood provide a load generator we can run in our VPC?
[05:55] Samir: Yes, we have a harness repo with a dockerized load-generator that supports open/closed loop, configurable concurrency, and prompt fixtures. We'll share an example K8s job manifest to run it in-cluster.
[06:06] Laura: Will the harness generate per-request metadata so we can correlate with our traces?
[06:09] Leah: Yes, it emits request IDs and supports sending trace headers so you can join traces in your observability stack.
[06:16] Priya: For quant tests, will you provide prebuilt quantized artifacts?
[06:19] Samir: We can provide recommended quant profiles and, for the models we host, prebuilt quantized variants; for on-prem we'll provide the quantization pipeline to reproduce locally. Document the exact build steps.
[06:30] Michael: Any advice on measuring tokenization cost separately? We saw tokenization taking non-trivial CPU time.
[06:34] Leah: Instrument tokenization as a separate timing metric. Run tokenization as a pre-step for some runs to isolate its cost, and for others include it inline to measure end-to-end. If tokenization dominates, consider using a tokenization service colocated with the runtime.
[06:46] Laura: For reporting, format wise — what do you usually include in the deliverable?
[06:49] Samir: We produce a runbook, the raw metrics (CSV), analysis notebook, cost projections, and recommendations (batching/quant/warmup). We'll also include suggested config files to reproduce results.
[07:00] Priya: Can we get an example bench that shows how caching changes throughput for long chat?
[07:04] Leah: Yes we'll include a sample that runs long-chat sessions with and without session-level KV caching and show throughput vs p99. It typically shows a 2-3x effective throughput improvement for high-reuse sessions.
[07:16] Michael: What about autoscaling and burst capacity — do you factor that into cost?
[07:20] Samir: We model steady-state and burst scenarios. Autoscaling policies impact tail latency when scaling cold; we include a warm standby or burst pool in some configs to model lower p99 for bursts. We'll show trade-offs in cost model.
[07:33] Laura: Could you clarify the recommended GPU metrics sampling frequency?
[07:36] Leah: 1s sampling is fine for throughput and utilization. For kernel-level details you might need sub-second, but 1s is normally sufficient.
[07:45] Priya: Are there specific sequence patterns that break 4-bit quantization more than others?
[07:49] Leah: Numeric stability issues sometimes appear for long sequences or when activations have high dynamic range; we flag sequences where log-prob deltas exceed a threshold. We'll include a small test suite for that.
[08:01] Michael: Regarding test reproducibility, do you recommend containerizing the entire pipeline?
[08:05] Samir: Yes, containerize load generator and runtime environment, pin dependencies, and record environment checksums. Also record hardware counters and driver versions.
[08:15] Laura: For VPC network tests, do you add artificial latency to simulate cross-region?
[08:18] Leah: You can. Use tc/netem to inject latency and packet loss to simulate WAN conditions; run both baseline and degraded network tests.
[08:28] Priya: When we run the baseline, what sample size do you recommend for stable p99 estimates?
[08:32] Samir: At least 10 minutes of steady-state per trial and 3+ trials; if p99 is unstable, extend run length. Use bootstrap to compute confidence intervals.
[08:41] Michael: Any standard naming for configs so we can compare results across runs?
[08:45] Leah: We suggest a naming convention: model-seq-batch-quant-window-concurrency-date (e.g., gptx-512-b32-int8-25ms-8-20261005). We'll include a parser in the harness.
[08:58] Laura: Let's talk about output logging — how big are the metric CSVs? Any perf impact?
[09:02] Samir: High-frequency logging can add overhead; write metrics to local files first and flush periodically. Use sample-based logging for kernel traces. The harness supports configurable sampling.
[09:13] Priya: For on-prem we'll need to coordinate maintenance windows for runs to avoid interference.
[09:17] Michael: Ok timeline-wise, we want to run an initial apples-to-apples within two weeks.
[09:21] Samir: Great. We'll share the repo and a runbook by Friday. Leah and I will help run the first benchmark in your VPC.
[09:27] Leah: We'll also prepare a minimal set of scripts to collect GPU counters and system metrics.
[09:33] Laura: Do you have any benchmark examples comparing 4bit vs fp16 throughput?
[09:37] Leah: Yes we have internal examples showing throughput improvements at 4-bit with small quality regressions in edge cases; we'll share those with calibration notes.
[09:47] Priya: Any quick tips to reduce noise during runs?
[09:50] Samir: Pin CPUs, disable unnecessary daemons, isolate NICs, and schedule runs during low cluster activity. Also use dedicated test accounts to avoid throttling from shared quotas.
[10:02] Michael: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[10:05] Samir: Recap: Samir share harness + runbook by 2026-10-08; Laura provision test infra by 2026-10-07; Leah and Priya run baseline and report by 2026-10-15; Samir produce cost worksheet by 2026-10-12.
[10:18] Laura: Thanks everyone. We'll get access details to you later today.
[10:22] Priya: Appreciate it. Looking forward to the hands-on.
[10:25] Samir: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links. Bye.
[10:30] (call ends)
